analysis.one_liner: Extends the federal tariff on imported ethanol two more years and orders a study of Caribbean imports.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend an added federal import duty on ethanol—about 54 cents per gallon under the tariff schedule—through January 1, 2011, two years past its scheduled end [S2][S3]. That duty makes foreign ethanol, mainly Brazilian sugarcane ethanol, more expensive than domestic corn ethanol [S2]. It would also order the Treasury Department to study whether ethanol from countries like Brazil is entering the United States duty-free by routing through Caribbean countries that hold duty-free status, and to report to Congress [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic corn ethanol producers and corn farmers in states like South Dakota, who are shielded from cheaper foreign ethanol by the import duty. Fuel blenders would face no new tariff costs avoided... rather, they would pay them: the tariff is a cost passed on in fuel prices, so its beneficiaries are the domestic ethanol industry and its farm suppliers.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the added import duty on ethanol, scheduled to expire January 1, 2009, through January 1, 2011, keeping foreign ethanol more expensive than domestic corn ethanol [S2][S3].

Orders a Treasury study of how much ethanol is entering the United States duty-free through Caribbean Basin beneficiary countries, including where that ethanol originates and what would happen to the domestic industry if the duty-free quota treatment ended [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Drivers and fuel blenders. Because federal rules require ethanol to be blended into gasoline, a tariff on imported ethanol raises the price of a required fuel ingredient, and the cost lands in pump prices. Caribbean economies that process and export ethanol duty-free would also bear costs, as would foreign ethanol producers like Brazil.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drivers, fuel blenders, and Caribbean exporters

drawbacks.text: The tariff raises the price of a fuel that federal mandates require blenders to use, so its cost is passed to consumers at the pump rather than absorbed by importers [S2][S3].

Keeping foreign ethanol out limits supply in a market where domestic production cannot always meet demand, which blenders and livestock feed users have argued raises their costs; this is the standard cost of import protection and the bill offers no offsetting relief [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is straightforward import protection: it preserves a price advantage for domestic ethanol at the direct expense of anyone who buys fuel. The study component is harmless and arguably useful, but the core purpose of the bill is to keep a cheaper foreign product more expensive for two more years.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Thune introduced the bill on April 12, 2007, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S1][S5].
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no cosponsors joined [S4][S5].
The bill died at the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009, without ever reaching the Senate floor [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drivers, fuel blenders, and foreign ethanol producers were better off because the tariff extension never advanced; the domestic ethanol industry did not get its two extra years of guaranteed price protection.

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.role: U.S. Senator from South Dakota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the ethanol import tariff through 2011 and to require a Treasury study of Caribbean ethanol transshipment [S1][S3][S5].

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; chaired by Sen. Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it sat in committee from April 2007 until the Congress ended with no action beyond the initial referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the partisan shape of support and opposition cannot be measured from the record [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Domestic corn ethanol producers and corn growers
industries.note: The extended tariff keeps their main foreign competitor—cheaper imported ethanol—more expensive, protecting sales and prices for a home-state industry. Because ethanol must be blended into gasoline by law, the tariff's cost flows into fuel prices paid by drivers.

industries.industry: Caribbean ethanol refiners and foreign ethanol producers (chiefly Brazil)
industries.note: The tariff extension keeps their ethanol priced out of the U.S. market, and the study is aimed at closing duty-free routing through Caribbean countries. Cheap foreign ethanol would otherwise lower fuel costs for American consumers.
They are required to blend ethanol into gasoline, so a tariff on imported ethanol raises the price of a mandatory input, which they pass to consumers.
